summary:
HESTIA is an offline health self-monitoring tool for astronauts on long missions, built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (ESGI Paris).
On Mars, a message to Earth can take up to about 22 minutes each way, so the crew must be able to judge their own health and supplies without waiting for mission control.
A station computer (React/Tauri desktop app) gathers every crew member's data on a FastAPI + SQLite server that runs locally, with no network.
Each astronaut logs sleep, mood, symptoms, meals and a reaction-time test from a phone app, by scanning a QR code shown on the station.
A local vision model (Qwen 2.5 VL through Ollama) reads photos of the food shelf to estimate stock, and the crew confirms or corrects each estimate.
The station shows each crew member's status, explaining why someone is flagged and whether each value is measured, declared, estimated or simulated.
The Earth link simulates the communication delay and gives the crew an onboard plan of what to do while the answer is on its way.
The management simulator tests decisions in five steps (for example, a cargo arriving 90 days late) and produces a report of critical items and items to watch.
Figures come from cited sources (NASA Human Research Program, NASA-STD-3001, Curiosity's radiation measurements, Canadian Space Agency) or are marked as assumptions.
HESTIA is not a medical device: it makes no diagnosis, names no drugs or doses, and all crew data is fictional and labelled SIMULATED.
details:
HESTIA lets an astronaut crew check its own health and food supply when Earth cannot answer in time; on Mars, a message can take up to 22 minutes each way.
Each crew member logs vital signs, sleep, mood, symptoms, meals and a short reaction test on a phone, and the station combines this into a body silhouette with green, orange or red zones.
A local vision model reads photos of the food shelf to estimate the stock, and a person confirms or corrects each count before it is saved.
Orange gives short self-care advice and red alerts the crew. A short report goes to Earth only for a critical value or two red indicators, and the station shows an onboard plan while the reply is on its way.
A management simulator tests a decision in five steps, such as a cargo arriving 90 days late, and reports what becomes critical and what needs watching.
The benefit is autonomy: the crew acts as its own first line of mission control, sees early which hazards are rising, and keeps clear of the communication delay.
The intended impact is a crew that knows why each measurement matters and what to do next, while every value is clearly marked as measured, declared, estimated or simulated.
We built it with Python (FastAPI, SQLModel, SQLite, OpenCV), React and TypeScript, Tauri for the desktop station, Capacitor for iOS, and Ollama running Qwen 2.5 VL locally on a MacBook, with iPhones as crew devices.
It is creative because it works with no network at all: a single laptop holds the server, the AI and the apps, and the phones join over the base Wi-Fi by scanning a QR code.
We considered the NASA Human Research Program hazards, NASA-STD-3001, Curiosity's radiation data, privacy, offline use, colour paired with an icon and a word for readability, and honesty: HESTIA is not a medical device and its crew data is simulated.

Video presentation of the project : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9PFC_OzkaCY&feature=youtu.be
